title: Does AI speak your language?
essentialQuestion: Why does AI work better in some languages than others, and what are people doing about it?
learningGoal: Explain why AI tools work better in some languages than others, and describe how communities are building tools for their own languages.

warmUp.question: A tool learns from lots of writing, and most of it is in one language. What do you think happens?
options: It works best in that language
It works the same in every language

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Which language has the most speakers? Which language has the most writing online?

cards.title: Three languages at the Harbourside bus station

cards.title: The bus station's help screen
items: You type a question, such as “When is the next bus to the market?”
An AI tool reads the question and writes an answer.
It learned from writing taken from the internet.

activity.title: Test the Harbourside help screen
activity.instructions: The Harbourside team asked the help screen the same 20 questions in each language. Tap the language it got wrong most often.

afterTap.question: Why did the help screen make the most mistakes in Language C?

options.text: Very few people speak Language C
options.feedback: Not quite. Language C has the most speakers in the region. Look at how much writing it has online.

options.text: Language C is a harder language
options.feedback: Not quite. No language is worse or harder for a tool. The tool just had fewer examples to learn from.

options.text: It learned from very little writing in Language C
options.feedback: Yes. Language C has very little writing online, so the tool had few examples to learn from.

activity.extension: Paper version: read out the three results, ask which language had the most mistakes, then ask the question above. Point back to the evidence table: Language C has the most speakers but the least writing online.
activity.saves: The learner's answer, with the lesson's other answers.

sections.heading: AI learns languages from writing
sections.text: AI tools that write, answer questions or translate learn from training data. For these tools, the data is a huge amount of writing, much of it from the internet. People speak more than 7,000 languages, but most big AI tools learned mainly from English. A language with little writing online is called a low-resource language. It can still have many speakers. About 200 million people speak Swahili, but there is not enough Swahili writing online for AI to learn well. In Harbourside, the help screen works well in Language A. It makes many mistakes in Language C, though more people there speak it.
sections.simpler: Some AI tools write, answer questions or translate. They learn from training data. This data is lots of writing from the web. People speak more than 7,000 languages. But most big AI tools learned from English. Some languages have little writing online. We call this a low-resource language. It can still have many speakers. About 200 million people speak Swahili. But there is not much written in it online. The Harbourside help screen works well in Language A. It makes many mistakes in Language C.

sections.heading: Who gets left out, and why
sections.text: When a tool works badly in a language, its speakers get worse help. Researchers warn that health or work tools that only work well in English could leave many people out. How much writing a language has online is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools and offices mostly use Languages A and B. So little is written in Language C. Masakhane is a group of African researchers. It says African languages have a small place in technology partly because of colonialism. That was when other countries ruled much of Africa. So the people who build AI tools also decide which languages count.
sections.simpler: A tool can work badly in a language. Then its speakers get worse help. This is linked to history and power. In the town, schools use Language A. So there is little writing in Language C. Some African experts say the past matters too. Long ago, other countries ruled much of Africa. That is one reason their languages are left out. People who build AI choose which languages count.

sections.heading: People build tools for their own languages
sections.text: Now many people are building tools for their own languages. In Singapore, a government-led programme built a model called SEA-LION. Its first version learned from 11 Southeast Asian languages, such as Thai and Vietnamese. In Jakarta in 2024, two companies launched Sahabat-AI. It is made for Bahasa Indonesia and local languages such as Javanese. Masakhane's name means “We build together” in the isiZulu language. Its members build tools for African languages, with the people who speak them. When speakers help to build a tool, it fits their community better. But these tools still make mistakes, so people must keep checking them.
sections.simpler: Now people build tools for their own languages. A team in Singapore made SEA-LION. It learned from 11 languages of Southeast Asia. In 2024, a tool called Sahabat-AI started in Jakarta. The name Masakhane means “We build together”. This group makes tools for African languages. When speakers help, a tool fits their community better. But the tools still make mistakes. So people must check them.

glossary.definition: The examples a computer learns from.
glossary.example: The help screen's training data had very little writing in Language C.

glossary.definition: A language with only a little writing online for computers to learn from.
glossary.example: Language C is a low-resource language, but many people speak it.

glossary.definition: To change words from one language into another.
glossary.example: A tool that translates well in one language may make mistakes in another.

glossary.definition: The ability to decide what happens or to control things.
glossary.example: The people who build AI tools have the power to choose which languages they include.

glossary.definition: A group of people who live in the same place or share something.

options.text: A language that very few people speak
options.feedback: Not quite. About 200 million people speak Swahili, and it is still low-resource. Read the first section again.

options.text: A language with little writing online
options.feedback: Yes. A low-resource language has only a little writing online for AI tools to learn from.

options.text: A language that is very hard to learn
options.feedback: Not quite. It is not about how hard a language is. Look at what AI tools learn from.

checks.question: How are some people making AI work better in more languages?

options.text: They ask everyone to use only English
options.feedback: Not quite. The lesson shows people changing the tools, not their languages. Read the third section.

options.text: They stop using AI tools for any language
options.feedback: Not quite. People keep using the tools and make them better. Read the third section.

options.text: They build tools for their own languages
options.feedback: Yes. Groups like AI Singapore and Masakhane build tools with the people who speak the languages.

write.prompt: Use the Harbourside test to explain why an AI tool can work better in some languages than others. Then say who should help to fix it, and why.
sentenceStarters: The help screen worked best in ...
It made the most mistakes in ___, because ...
To fix it, ___ should help, because ...
selfCheck: I explained why the tool worked better in one language.
I said why this matters for the people who speak Language C.
I said who should help to fix it, and why.
write.example: The help screen worked best in Language A. It answered 19 of 20 questions well. It made the most mistakes in Language C, because its training data had very little writing in that language. This is unfair because more people in the region speak Language C, but they get worse help. To fix it, people who speak Language C should help, because they know it best. They could share writing and check the answers. This is like the Masakhane group, which builds tools for African languages.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner asks why an AI tool works worse in some languages. You answer with one reason from the lesson. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud what a low-resource language is. Then name one group from the lesson that builds tools for its own languages.

watch.title: Why AI doesn't speak every language
watch.why: It shows, with real examples, why AI tools learn much more about a few big languages than about most others, and what some people are doing about it.
watch.beforeQuestion: Why do you think an AI tool might know more about some languages than others?
watch.afterQuestion: Who decides which languages an AI tool learns from, according to the video?
watch.summary: This video asks why AI tools work better in some languages than in others. A tool like a chatbot learns by reading lots of writing. The video says it is like a giant bookshop. But the bookshop has a problem. Most of its books are in English and a few other big languages. Languages with little writing online are called low-resource languages. The tools know much less about them. The video looks at two of these, Jamaican Patois and Catalan. It also shows researchers who built an open model in many languages, with help from local communities. The presenter says a few big companies decide what goes into these tools. He says it matters to everyone that AI tools include many languages.
keyPoints: AI tools learn mostly from writing in a few big languages, especially English.
Languages with little writing online get worse results.
Some researchers work with communities to include more languages.
watch.contentNote: Vox, 2023. Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed (October 2026); the length is not confirmed (a transcript archive suggests about 11 to 12 minutes, longer than most Thinkerwell videos). It names large technology companies, mentions a complaint about a search engine and Catalan, and the presenter talks about a voice assistant not understanding his accent. The summary was written from Rosetta's transcript archive of the video, not from watching it. Someone on the team must watch it before use; learners can read the written summary instead.

visual.description: PLACEHOLDER: no picture exists yet, and visuals/DW07.svg is only a planned path. Three columns, one for each Harbourside language, labelled “Language A”, “Language B” and “Language C”. In each column, a stack of pages shows how much writing is online: tall for A, middle for B, very short for C, each labelled in words (“Lots of writing”, “Some writing”, “Very little writing”). Under each stack, a row of simple figures shows the speakers: the row under C is the longest, labelled “Most speakers”. At the bottom of each column, the help screen's result is written in words and digits (19 of 20, 15 of 20, 6 of 20), so colour is never the only clue. Simple drawn figures only; no flags, maps or real alphabets.
visual.alt: A diagram of three languages. Language A has lots of writing online and the help screen gets 19 of 20 right. Language C has the most speakers but very little writing, and gets only 6 of 20 right.

sensitiveNotes: Many learners speak several languages, and some speak a low-resource language. Never ask which languages learners or their families speak, or where they come from; let them share only if they choose. Make clear that no language is worse or simpler: the gap is about how much writing computers had to learn from, and who chose it.
The second section mentions colonialism briefly, as Masakhane does. Keep any discussion short and factual, and don't ask learners about their own history or any country's politics.
educatorNotes: The Harbourside results (19, 15 and 6 of 20) are made up. The real facts come from the sources: Stanford researchers on low-resource languages and Swahili; Context (2024) on SEA-LION, which also reports that about 63% of SEA-LION's training text was still English, and that critics worry regional models can repeat the views of powerful groups; GoTo's press release on Sahabat-AI (launched in Jakarta, November 2024, with Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison); and Masakhane's listing. Meta's NLLB-200 model translates 200 languages, about three-quarters of them low-resource (MultiLingual). Older learners could discuss who owns these tools.

For the Jakarta pilot, Sahabat-AI's languages (Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and Sundanese) are a local link, but learners never need to name a language they speak. Lesson 8 comes back to the same cause (missing examples) and calls it bias.
changes: New lesson (Digital World, October 2026, social studies rebuild). There is no Base44 original, so oldId is null. Lesson 7 in “Who builds AI, and at what cost” (who-builds-ai).

Social studies angle: language and power, who gets left out, and who decides which languages count. It names real projects (SEA-LION, Sahabat-AI, Masakhane) in the Read text as facts, as the rebuild brief allows; every example learners work with is made up (Harbourside, Languages A, B and C).
Adds a compare-results activity (a made-up help screen tested in three made-up languages).
